paragraphs.heading: What velocity is
paragraphs.text: Velocity tells you how fast something is moving and in which direction. It is a core idea in kinematics, the branch of classical mechanics that describes how physical objects move. Because you need both a size and a direction to state it, velocity is a vector quantity.

paragraphs.heading: Speed versus velocity
paragraphs.text: In everyday talk people often use speed and velocity as if they meant the same thing, but in physics they differ. Speed is just the size of the velocity, so it says how fast but not which way. "5 metres per second" is a speed, a scalar, while "5 metres per second east" is a velocity, a vector. In the SI system both are measured in metres per second.

paragraphs.heading: Steady velocity and acceleration
paragraphs.text: An object keeps a constant velocity only if its speed and its direction both stay the same. That means it moves in a straight line at a steady speed. Any change in speed, direction or both is called acceleration. A car driving round a circle at a steady 20 kilometres per hour keeps its speed but not its velocity, since its direction keeps changing, so it is accelerating.

paragraphs.heading: Average and instantaneous
paragraphs.text: Average velocity over a stretch of time is the change in position, Δs, divided by the time taken, Δt, written v̄ = Δs/Δt. Instantaneous velocity can be pictured as the velocity an object would keep if it stopped accelerating at that moment. On a graph of position against time, the instantaneous velocity is the slope of the tangent line at a point, and the average velocity is the slope of the secant line joining the start and end of the period. Average velocity is never larger than average speed, because distance only ever grows while displacement can shrink or change direction.

paragraphs.heading: Linked to acceleration
paragraphs.text: Acceleration at a given instant is how fast velocity changes over time, written as a derivative, 𝒂 = d𝒗/dt. When the acceleration is constant, velocity can be worked out with the suvat equations. One of them is 𝒗 = 𝒖 + 𝒂t, where u is the velocity at time t = 0 and v the velocity at time t. These equations hold in both Newtonian mechanics and special relativity.

paragraphs.heading: Momentum, energy and escape
paragraphs.text: Velocity feeds into other key quantities. Momentum is mass times velocity, 𝒑 = m𝒗, a vector. Kinetic energy, Eₖ = 1/2mv², is a scalar, since it depends on the square of the velocity. Escape velocity is the minimum speed an object needs to break free of a massive body such as Earth. From Earth's surface it is about 11 200 m/s whatever the direction, which makes "escape speed" the more accurate name.

paragraphs.heading: Relative velocity
paragraphs.text: Relative velocity compares the motion of two objects measured in a single coordinate system. If object A moves with velocity v and object B with velocity w, the velocity of A relative to B is the difference, v − w. In Newtonian mechanics this answer does not depend on which inertial reference frame you choose. In special relativity it does.
